overview.title: Functional API as default; the standard training workflow
overview.section: 7.3 Using built-in training and evaluation loops
overview.main_topic: The book's choice of Functional models with subclassed layers, and the compile/fit/evaluate/predict workflow as the simplest point on the training spectrum
overview.central_idea: From here on the book uses Functional models, often containing subclassed layers, for the best of both worlds. Training follows the same progressive disclosure of complexity as model building, and its simplest form is Listing 7.17's compile() → fit() → evaluate() → predict() on MNIST.
overview.importance: Listing 7.17 is the baseline that sections 7.3 and 7.4 will customize step by step: custom metrics, callbacks, TensorBoard, custom train_step() and fully custom loops. get_mnist_model() is factored into a function precisely so it can be reused there.
learning_objectives: State the book's model-building convention for the rest of the book and its rationale
Explain how progressive disclosure of complexity applies to training

Compute the tensor shapes, parameter counts and data split sizes in Listing 7.17

summary:
The page first closes section 7.2. **From now on, every example in the book uses the Functional API**, because every model the book builds is expressible as a graph of layers, while making frequent use of **subclassed layers**. Functional models with subclassed layers inside give "the best of both worlds": high development flexibility while keeping the Functional API's advantages, such as layer connectivity for plotting and feature extraction (p.229).

Section **7.3, "Using built-in training and evaluation loops,"** applies the principle of **progressive disclosure of complexity** to training. Model building ranged from Sequential to subclassing. Training likewise ranges from just calling `fit()` to writing a brand-new training algorithm from scratch (the later part of the chapter, 7.4).

As a reminder of the simplest end, **Listing 7.17** shows the standard workflow on MNIST:

- `get_mnist_model()` builds a Functional model: `Input(shape=(28*28,))` → `Dense(512, relu)` → `Dropout(0.5)` → `Dense(10, softmax)`. It is wrapped in a function "so as to reuse it later."
- The data is loaded with `mnist.load_data()`, flattened to 784-vectors and scaled to [0, 1] by dividing the `float32` values by 255. The first 10,000 training images are **reserved for validation**, leaving 50,000 for training. The 10,000 test images are kept separate.
- `compile()` specifies the **optimizer** (`"adam"`), the **loss** to minimize (`"sparse_categorical_crossentropy"`, for integer labels) and the **metrics** to monitor (`["accuracy"]`).
- `fit()` trains for 3 epochs, with `validation_data` used to monitor performance on unseen data.
- `evaluate()` computes loss and metrics on new data. `predict()` returns class probabilities for new data.

The next page (p.231) lists the first two ways to customize this workflow: custom metrics and callbacks.

paragraphs.excerpt: Going forward, all examples in this book will use the Functional API—simply
paragraphs.what_it_says: All examples from now on use the Functional API, because every model in the book can be expressed as a graph of layers. Subclassed layers will be used frequently. Functional models containing subclassed layers give the best of both worlds: high development flexibility and the advantages of the Functional API.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the practical outcome of the 7.2 discussion. Custom computation goes into small, self-contained Layer subclasses, and those layers are wired together with the Functional API. Each custom layer becomes one node in an inspectable graph, so you still get summary() connectivity, plot_model() and feature extraction at the model level.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells you what code style to expect in the rest of the book. Later Transformer, convnet and generative models will be Functional graphs built from custom layers.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Opaque code is confined to layer internals and the overall topology stays explicit, which follows the 'right tool for the job' rule (p.229).

terminology.meaning: A custom layer defined by inheriting from keras.Layer and implementing build()/call().
Flexibility of custom code together with the inspectability of a graph.

connections: p.229: prefer the Functional API when the model is a DAG of layers
p.228: what subclassed models don't support

paragraphs.excerpt: The principle of progressive disclosure of complexity—access to a spectrum of workflows
paragraphs.what_it_says: Progressive disclosure of complexity, a spectrum of workflows from dead easy to arbitrarily flexible taken one step at a time, also applies to training. Keras training can be as simple as calling fit() or as advanced as writing a new training algorithm from scratch.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Training has its own ladder, parallel to the one for model building (Sequential → Functional → subclassing). Its rungs are: built-in fit(); fit() customized with metrics and callbacks (7.3.1-7.3.3); fit() with a custom train_step() (7.4.4-7.4.5); fully custom loops (7.4.2). Each rung keeps you within the same Keras objects, so you add only the complexity you need.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the organizing principle of the rest of chapter 7.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: the key design point is that higher rungs reuse lower-level pieces (metrics, optimizers, losses) instead of replacing them.

terminology.meaning: Simple things are simple; complex things are possible; you move between them incrementally (p.215-216).

connections: p.216: figure 7.1, progressive disclosure for model building
p.254: summary, overriding train_step() and writing training loops from scratch

concepts.name: Functional API
concepts.definition: Building models by calling layers on symbolic tensors from keras.Input, producing an explicit graph of layers.
concepts.intuition: A wiring diagram whose boxes can themselves be custom-built.
concepts.technical: get_mnist_model() is a Functional model: Input → Dense → Dropout → Dense, wrapped with keras.Model(inputs, outputs).
concepts.significance: The book's convention for all remaining examples.
concepts.misconception: That the Functional API rules out custom code. Subclassed layers are used inside Functional models throughout the book.

concepts.name: Progressive disclosure of complexity
concepts.definition: Keras's design principle of offering a spectrum of workflows from very simple to arbitrarily flexible, reachable one step at a time.
concepts.intuition: A staircase rather than a cliff: each step adds a bit of control.
concepts.technical: For training: fit() → custom metrics/callbacks → custom train_step() → custom loops, all sharing Keras components.
concepts.significance: Lets beginners and researchers use the same framework.
concepts.example: Using Listing 7.17 as is, then adding a custom metric (p.231).
concepts.misconception: That advanced workflows require leaving Keras for raw backend code. They mix Keras objects with backend APIs.

concepts.name: Validation set
concepts.definition: Data held out from training to monitor generalization during training.
concepts.intuition: A practice exam you don't study from.
concepts.technical: Listing 7.17 slices the first 10,000 of the 60,000 MNIST training images as validation data and passes them via validation_data, so fit() reports val_loss and val_accuracy each epoch.
concepts.significance: Separates model selection from the final test evaluation.
concepts.misconception: That the test set can double as validation data. Repeated tuning on it leaks information.

concepts.name: Dropout
concepts.definition: A layer that randomly zeroes a fraction of its inputs during training.
concepts.intuition: Forcing the network not to rely on any single unit.
concepts.technical: Dropout(0.5) zeroes 50% of the 512 features at training time (scaling the rest by 1/(1-0.5)) and does nothing at inference.
concepts.significance: Regularizes the 512-unit hidden layer of get_mnist_model().
concepts.misconception: That dropout is active during evaluate()/predict(). It is only active in training mode.

concepts.name: compile/fit/evaluate/predict
concepts.definition: The four built-in Model methods that configure, train, assess and run a model.
concepts.intuition: Set up, practise, take the exam, then use what you've learned.
concepts.technical: compile(optimizer, loss, metrics); fit(x, y, epochs, validation_data); evaluate(x, y) returns loss plus metrics; predict(x) returns outputs.
concepts.significance: The simplest end of the training spectrum and the baseline for the rest of chapter 7.
concepts.misconception: That predict() returns class labels. Here it returns softmax probabilities; take argmax for labels.

math.title: Pixel flattening and scaling

variables.meaning: One 28×28 grayscale MNIST image with uint8 intensities 0-255
The image flattened row by row into a 784-dimensional vector (reshape)
The float32 input vector fed to keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))

math.operations: Reshape (60000, 28, 28) → (60000, 784), cast to float32, divide elementwise by 255.
math.purpose: Match the model's flat input shape and put inputs on a small, consistent scale for stable optimization.
math.intuition: Neural networks train best when inputs are small numbers of similar magnitude.
math.numerical_example: A pixel value of 128 becomes 128/255 ≈ 0.502; 255 becomes 1.0; 0 stays 0.

math.title: Model computed by get_mnist_model()

variables.meaning: First Dense layer kernel (784×512) and bias (512)
Output Dense layer kernel (512×10) and bias (10)
Randomly zeroes half the features during training only

math.operations: Affine map, ReLU, dropout, affine map, softmax.
math.purpose: Map a flattened digit image to a probability distribution over the 10 digits.
math.interpretation: predict() returns ŷ for each test image.
math.intuition: One hidden layer of 512 features, regularized by dropout, then a 10-way probabilistic classifier.
math.numerical_example: Parameters: 784·512 + 512 = 401,920 in the hidden layer; 512·10 + 10 = 5,130 in the output; total 407,050. Dropout has none.

code.title: Listing 7.17: The standard workflow: compile(), fit(), evaluate(), predict()
code.original_code:
from keras.datasets import mnist

def get_mnist_model():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28 * 28,))
    features = layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")(inputs)
    features = layers.Dropout(0.5)(features)
    outputs = layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax")(features)
    model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
    return model

(images, labels), (test_images, test_labels) = mnist.load_data()
images = images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28)).astype("float32") / 255
test_images = test_images.reshape((10000, 28 * 28)).astype("float32") / 255
train_images, val_images = images[10000:], images[:10000]
train_labels, val_labels = labels[10000:], labels[:10000]

model = get_mnist_model()
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
model.fit(
    train_images,
    train_labels,
    epochs=3,
    validation_data=(val_images, val_labels),
)
test_metrics = model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)
predictions = model.predict(test_images)
code.what_it_does: Defines a reusable Functional MNIST classifier, prepares the data with a validation split, then compiles, trains, evaluates and predicts.

line_explanations.explanation: Callout: 'Creates a model. (We factor this into a separate function so as to reuse it later.)' Functional graph: (None, 784) → Dense(512, relu) → Dropout(0.5) → Dense(10, softmax).

Callout: 'Loads your data, reserving some for validation.' Flatten and scale both training (60,000) and test (10,000) images. The first 10,000 training samples become validation data and the remaining 50,000 are used for training.

Callout: 'Compiles the model by specifying its optimizer, the loss function to minimize, and metrics to monitor.' Adam optimizer, sparse categorical crossentropy (integer labels 0-9), accuracy metric.

Callout: 'Uses fit() to train the model, optionally providing validation data to monitor performance on unseen data.' 3 epochs over the 50,000 training samples, with the default batch size of 32 (not set here).
Callout: 'Uses evaluate() to compute the loss and metrics on new data.' Returns [loss, accuracy] on the test set.
Callout: 'Uses predict() to compute classification probabilities on new data.' predictions has shape (10000, 10).

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: MNIST uint8 images (60000, 28, 28) and (10000, 28, 28) with integer labels. Outputs: a training History (not stored here), test_metrics = [loss, accuracy], predictions of shape (10000, 10).
code.algorithm: Mini-batch gradient descent with Adam minimizing crossentropy, with validation metrics computed at the end of each epoch.
code.theory_link: The simplest point on the training spectrum, which the rest of chapter 7 customizes.

parameters.name: optimizer="adam"
parameters.role: Adaptive-moment gradient optimizer with default learning rate.

parameters.name: loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy"
parameters.role: Crossentropy for integer class labels against softmax outputs.

parameters.name: metrics=["accuracy"]
parameters.role: Fraction of correctly classified samples, reported during fit and evaluate.

parameters.name: epochs=3
parameters.role: Number of full passes over the training data.

parameters.name: validation_data
parameters.role: Held-out (val_images, val_labels) evaluated after each epoch.

parameters.name: Dropout(0.5)
parameters.role: Drops half of the hidden features during training.

pitfalls: Using categorical_crossentropy with integer labels: the labels would have to be one-hot encoded.
Slicing the validation set from the training data after shuffling it independently of the labels misaligns them; here images and labels are sliced identically.
predict() outputs probabilities, so use predictions.argmax(axis=-1) for digit labels.
The listing assumes `import keras` and `from keras import layers` were run earlier in the chapter.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: inspect results of Listing 7.17
print(test_metrics)               # [test_loss, test_accuracy]
print(predictions.shape)          # (10000, 10)
predicted_digits = predictions.argmax(axis=-1)
print((predicted_digits == test_labels).mean())  # matches test accuracy

deeper.title: The training ladder this section opens
deeper.body:
Based on the chapter outline:

1. **Built-in loop**: `compile()` + `fit()` (this page).
2. **Custom metrics**: subclass `keras.metrics.Metric` (7.3.1, p.231).
3. **Callbacks**: act at points during training (7.3.2-7.3.3, p.232-234).
4. **TensorBoard** monitoring (7.3.4, p.236).
5. **Custom training step functions and loops** (7.4, p.238-245).
6. **fit() with a custom train_step()** (7.4.4-7.4.5, p.246-250).

Each step keeps as much of the built-in machinery as possible.

deeper.title: Steps per epoch
deeper.body: Beyond the book: with 50,000 training samples and Keras's default `batch_size=32`, one epoch is $\lceil 50000/32 \rceil = 1563$ gradient updates, so `epochs=3` gives about 4,689 updates. Validation then runs on 10,000 samples after each epoch.

deeper.title: Why wrap the model in a function?
deeper.body: The callout says `get_mnist_model()` is factored out "so as to reuse it later." Calling it returns a **fresh, untrained** model each time, with new random weights. Later experiments (custom metrics, callbacks, custom loops) can then start from the same architecture without leftovers from earlier training. Reusing one `model` object would continue training from its current weights.

takeaways: The book uses Functional models with subclassed layers from here on: flexibility plus Functional advantages.
Training also follows progressive disclosure of complexity, from fit() to custom training algorithms.
Listing 7.17 is the baseline: get_mnist_model(), a 50k/10k/10k data split, compile(adam, sparse CCE, accuracy), fit(3 epochs, validation_data), evaluate(), predict().
get_mnist_model() is a function so later sections can get a fresh model.
predict() returns class probabilities; evaluate() returns loss and metrics.

questions.question: Why does the book say all its remaining examples will use the Functional API?
options: Because subclassing is deprecated in Keras 3
Because all of the models the book works with are expressible as graphs of layers
Because the Functional API trains faster
Because subclassed layers cannot be used in Functional models
questions.answer: Because all of the models the book works with are expressible as graphs of layers
questions.explanation: That's the reason given. Subclassing isn't deprecated (p.226-229), speed isn't mentioned, and subclassed layers are explicitly used inside Functional models.

questions.question: How many samples are used for training, validation and testing in Listing 7.17?
questions.explanation: images[10000:] keeps 50,000 of the 60,000 training images. images[:10000] gives validation. The test set is the separate 10,000 images.

questions.question: Compute the number of trainable parameters in get_mnist_model().
questions.explanation: Dense(512) on 784 inputs: 784·512 + 512 = 401,920. Dense(10) on 512: 512·10 + 10 = 5,130. Dropout has no parameters. Total 407,050.

questions.question: Why is the loss "sparse_categorical_crossentropy" rather than "categorical_crossentropy"?
options: Because the labels are integers 0-9, not one-hot vectors
Because the output layer uses ReLU
Because the data is sparse after flattening
questions.answer: Because the labels are integers 0-9, not one-hot vectors
questions.explanation: MNIST labels from load_data() are integers, and the sparse variant accepts them directly. The output uses softmax, not ReLU. 'Sparse' refers to labels, not inputs. Epoch count is irrelevant.

questions.question: What does 'progressive disclosure of complexity' mean when applied to training, according to this page?
questions.answer: Keras offers a spectrum of training workflows, from simply calling fit() to writing a new training algorithm from scratch, which you can move along one step at a time.
questions.explanation: This is the first paragraph of 7.3, and it mirrors the model-building spectrum of 7.2.

questions.question: What does model.predict(test_images) return in Listing 7.17?
options: An array of shape (10000, 10) of class probabilities
An array of 10000 integer digit labels
questions.answer: An array of shape (10000, 10) of class probabilities
questions.explanation: The callout says predict() computes classification probabilities. Loss and accuracy come from evaluate(), labels need an argmax, and history comes from fit().
